edges.description: Without effective cell-mediated containment, ingested organisms that have crossed the gut progress to sustained bloodstream infection.
Organisms delivered to the gut use internalins to enter host cells and cross the intestinal epithelium.
Barrier entry lets Listeria survive in phagocytes and spread through the bloodstream.
InlA/InlB-associated barrier crossing can also seed the placenta and fetus during maternal invasive listeriosis.
Neonatal infection may progress through sepsis and bloodstream spread before meningeal invasion.
Bloodborne bacteria reach central nervous system barriers either through endothelial invasion or through infected leukocytes.
Endothelial crossing delivers the organism into the central nervous system compartment.
Organisms internalized in CNS myeloid or barrier cells must leave the phagocytic vesicle to complete the intracellular life cycle.
Cytosolic bacteria polymerize host actin and push into neighboring cells without requiring extracellular exposure.
Repeated intracellular spread and tissue invasion amplify local infection in the meninges and adjacent brain parenchyma.
Suppurative inflammation of the meninges and adjacent parenchyma is what presents clinically as meningoencephalitis, the dominant form of neurolisteriosis.
Ventricular involvement and inflammatory obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid flow produce contrast-enhancing ventricles or hydrocephalus in a minority of cases.
Brainstem and cerebellar localization of the suppurative process is what is seen on MRI as the rhombencephalitis pattern.

edges.description: The systemic inflammatory response to CNS and bloodstream infection presents as fever, which is near-universal on admission.

Parenchymal involvement of the brain by the suppurative process impairs the level of consciousness.
